w: What's tested Five of Exam 2's fifty questions come from Exam 1 material: L2, L3, L6 and L10 only How the five break down (from the class, November 11): two from L2, one on which hormones synergize, one on how PTH maintains blood calcium Below: the Exam 1 cram sheet for those four lectures The questions here are the Exam 1 hub's High Likelihood questions for those four lectures (Exam 1's predicted topics) Exam 2 has fifty questions: forty-five on the new lectures and five on Exam 1 material. Those five come from four Exam 1 lectures: L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary, L3 Endocrinology of Growth, L6 Adrenal Gland and L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation. So this refresher keeps the Exam 1 cram sheet for those four, and their questions are copies of the Exam 1 hub's High Likelihood questions. L1, L4, L5, L7, L8 and L9 aren't on Exam 2. The class also heard how the five break down: two from L2, one on which hormones work synergistically, and one on how PTH maintains blood calcium; the fifth wasn't named. Those three points are first in each list below. L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary Three hormone types: peptides (stored, surface receptors), amines, steroids (made on demand, cholesterol from LDL, intracellular receptors) Know Gs, Gi, Gq plus the insulin (RTK) and GH (JAK2) receptors Negative feedback is the hallmark: hormonal or physiologic response; short vs long loop Anterior: hypothalamic releasing hormones via the portal system Posterior: makes no hormones; oxytocin and ADH come down axons from supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei Dopamine holds prolactin down Releasing hormones come in pulses Primary: target hormone and pituitary hormone move opposite; secondary: same direction L3 Endocrinology of Growth Synergy: thyroid hormone (T3) works synergistically with GH on bone growth in children; T3 is on the growth plate slide with GH and IGF-1 GH: somatotrophs, 191 aa, pulses, biggest an hour after sleep onset GHRH (Gs) raises it; somatostatin (Gi, hyperpolarizes) lowers it: yin-yang Also up: ghrelin, sleep, stress; down: IGF-1, GH itself, glucose, free fatty acids Direct (MAPK/ERK, chondrocytes) vs IGF-1 (JAK-STAT, liver) Somatomedin hypothesis: GH needs a serum factor (IGF-1) GH is diabetogenic and lipolytic; builds muscle protein Not needed for fetal growth (insulin is) Estrogen closes the plates Gigantism before closure; acromegaly after (jaw, brow, hands); test IGF + glucose tolerance Somatopause: the hypothalamus (GHRH) GH matters all life long: muscle, organs, thymus and lymphocytes Insulin drives growth in utero (big babies of diabetic mothers) Growth plate: reserve (GH commits) → proliferation (IGF-1) → hypertrophy → apoptosis → ossification Main feedback: GH and IGF-1 raise hypothalamic somatostatin Acromegaly fertility trouble: too much SHBG, little free sex hormone Prof's focus (10/29): GH regulation, GH and IGF-1, metabolic effects, excess or deficiency, aging. Know the relationships. Somatopause: from the 30s, smaller and shorter pulses; the weak link is GHRH, not the somatotrophs L6 Adrenal Gland Cortex 90% (steroids), medulla (catecholamines); blood flows cortex → medulla Glomerulosa: aldosterone (only zone with aldosterone synthase) Fasciculata/reticularis: cortisol and androgens (DHEA) Lightning bolt 1: cholesterol desmolase, ACTH-driven, rate-limiting for cortisol Angiotensin II (Gq) and high K+ drive aldosterone; ACTH only a little Aldosterone: ENaC + Na/K pump: keep Na, lose K 11β-HSD turns cortisol to cortisone in the kidney Cortisol peaks at 7-8 am; raises glucose; suppresses immunity PNMT (cortisol-induced): about 80% epinephrine Addison's: high ACTH + MSH → pigmented gums 21-hydroxylase deficiency: salt wasting, virilization L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation Synergy: PTH and vitamin D (calcitriol) raise blood calcium together: PTH turns on 1α-hydroxylase, and calcitriol raises gut absorption How PTH maintains blood calcium: bone (through the osteoblasts, which signal the osteoclasts), the kidney (keep calcium, dump phosphate, turn on 1α) and the gut (through calcitriol); net calcium up, phosphate down Low calcium: nerves too excitable → tetany, Trousseau's sign Plasma Ca: 50% ionized, 40% bound, 10% complexed Three sites: gut, bone, kidney Osteoblasts: PTH, D3, estrogen receptors; osteoclasts: calcitonin Skin (UV) → D3; liver → 25-OH; kidney 1α → calcitriol (24 → inactive) 1α on: low Ca, PTH, low phosphate Calcitriol: gut channels, calbindin, basolateral pump CaSR is Gq; rising intracellular Ca INHIBITS PTH (the paradox) PTH: keep Ca, dump phosphate; bone via osteoblasts; net Ca up, P down Calcitonin: C cells, inhibits osteoclasts, not essential Rickets (child) vs osteomalacia (adult); postmenopausal osteoporosis Primary hyperparathyroidism: high PTH and Ca, low P, kidney stones, more in women Calcium and phosphate move together, EXCEPT the kidney under PTH (star it) Hypercalcemia: lethargy; hypocalcemia: tetany, Trousseau's, Chvostek's Calbindin: "very, very important" PTH receptor on osteoblasts, NOT osteoclasts (osteoclasts are hematopoietic) Need one parathyroid; thyroidectomy for goiter caused tetany and death Treat primary hyperparathyroidism: calcitonin, bisphosphonates
